graph_apply.title: Apply a batch of changes
graph_apply.description: Create, patch or delete stored records (entities) and their named groups of fields (components) in one atomic transaction: either every change is accepted or none is. `change` is an array of bundles, where a bundle is one entity’s components as one JSON object: {entity: {eid}, <component>: {<properties>}}, the same shape a client’s apply() takes. An omitted property is left unchanged, a null property is cleared, a null component is removed, and $delete: true deletes the entity. An eid is an entity’s unique string id. Generate the eid yourself, or write '$name' as the eid and read the eid the graph assigned from the result. Where this store keeps names, alias: {name: '<your name>'} beside a '$name' eid makes the write idempotent: writing the same name again patches the entity that already has it instead of creating a second one, and a name can be used wherever an eid can. A read-modify-write can state what it was based on: $was: {doc: {body: "<hash>"}}, for example, gives, per component and property, the SHA-256 of the value you read (null for “it had none”), and the whole batch is refused, naming the property and its current value, if that value has changed since. That is compare-and-set: two callers spending the same balance or claiming the same reward, and only one of them succeeds. The result is the transaction as applied, one bundle per entity: {entity: {eid, num}}, every component as written, the stamps the graph added (created, updated), and the '$alias' you named it by. Every entity that was deleted, including any deleted as a consequence, is returned as {entity, tombstone: {}} and nothing else. This tool’s input schema is the store’s vocabulary (schema): every component, property and type; graph_schema reports the same thing at length. The schema is open: a component or property declared after you connected still reaches the graph, and a property nobody declared is refused by the server. check: true is a dry run: every check is made and the whole transaction is then rolled back, so the result is what a kept write would have returned, with every '$name' resolved to the eid it would get, or the refusal, worded exactly as it would be for a kept write. That is how a plan of several entities and the relationships (edges) between them is proven before any of it is written. Documentation: https://yaks.app/docs/store.

change.description: bundles to apply together: each needs entity: {eid} and the component fields to write; omitted fields stay unchanged

check.description: true to validate without keeping the proposed changes and return what would have been written; default false

graph_query.title: Query entities
graph_query.description: Find stored records (entities) by filtering on their named groups of fields (components) and their properties. Returns bundles: JSON objects with entity: {eid} and the record’s component objects. A bundle carries the components the query names, by a filter on one ('.recipe', '.doc.title~=cake') or by asking for one without filtering on it ('?doc'), and no other: name each component you will read, or add * for all of them. A query that names no component ('.eid=T-12', a bare search word) answers whole. graph_show returns one entity whole. A query string selects the records: '.task.status=open&.filed.priority<3'. It is made of filters written as .component.property=value (or .property=value when unambiguous), joined with &, with lists (a,b), ranges (1..9), != for not equal, ~= for text containing a value, < or > comparisons, '.prop' for present and '!prop' for absent. Directives go in the same string: .order=, .limit=, and .refs=<id> for everything that references an entity. filters, if passed, are joined onto q with &. Documentation: https://yaks.app/docs/querying.

q.description: query filters, e.g. .task.status=open&.filed.priority<3; graph_schema lists the valid components and properties

filters.description: extra dot-params, joined onto q with &

limit.description: return at most this many entities

graph_show.title: Show entities
graph_show.description: Read one or more stored records (entities) by their unique string id (eid), each returned whole as its own bundle: a JSON object with entity: {eid} and every named group of fields (component) it has. Only the entities asked for come back; what references one is a query of its own, graph_query with .refs=<id>, and a relationship is an edge entity found the same way. This is lookup by identity, not search: pass eids, or the names entities are addressed by where this store keeps names (an eid wins over a name spelled the same way).

ids.description: the eids or names of the entities to read

graph_schema.title: Read the schema
graph_schema.description: Read this store’s vocabulary (schema): each component is a named group of fields attached to an entity, a stored record; its properties are those fields. Returns markdown to read and, as structured content, one JSON Schema document with each component’s entry under $defs, the same shape as a vocab.json. It answers at one of three levels of detail. With no arguments: the index, every component with its meaning and each property’s type. With component (one name or several): that component in full, as declared, with each property’s type and meaning, which properties are server-owned or unique, what it references, and an example value; the markdown adds what references it and an example bundle that writes it. With kind: the definition of a display category such as task, plus index entries for the components it is displayed with. If both kind and component are passed, kind selects the answer. The index says what exists; a component in full is enough to write it. Documentation: https://yaks.app/docs/components.

component.description: a component to read in full, or a list of them

kind.description: a display category declared by the schema, such as task; returns its definition and associated components

search.title: Search text
search.description: Full-text search over this store’s entities: the ones whose text matches, ranked best first, as bundles: JSON objects containing each record’s id and named groups of fields. Searches the text fields this server indexes. graph_query filters on known properties; this finds entities by what their text says Documentation: https://yaks.app/docs/querying.

limit.description: return at most this many entities
